title: The Silk Road
objective: After this level you can explain how the Silk Road linked China, Persia and Europe.
summary: The Silk Road was a 6,400 km network worked in stages by middlemen, carrying goods and religions. The Pax Mongolica made its routes safer in the 13th and 14th centuries.

cards.headline: Almost nobody travelled the whole Silk Road. That’s how it worked.
cards.body: It ran about 6,400 km, yet goods crossed it in stages, handled by middleman after middleman. Then the Mongols changed the rules of the road.

cards.headline: A relay, not a road
cards.body: The Silk Road was a network of routes, about 6,400 km long, linking China with the Mediterranean. Few people travelled all of it; goods were handled in stages by middlemen. Silk went west, while wool, gold and silver went east. Think of a relay race where the baton was a bale of silk.

cards.headline: Ideas in the luggage
cards.body: Beliefs travelled too. Buddhism, from India, reached China along the Silk Road, and so did Nestorian Christianity. Remember Level 65’s paper? Chinese sheets moved along these routes into Central Asia before the craft of making them did. The goods were silk; the passengers were ideas.

cards.headline: The Mongol peace
cards.body: In the 13th and 14th centuries the Silk Road revived under the Mongols. Historians call it the Pax Mongolica, a time of relative stability, trade and exchange. Despite the violence of the conquests, merchants, diplomats and scholars could cross Mongol lands with unprecedented security. The Mongols expanded the yam, a network of postal and supply stations, and merchants carrying paiza passes had imperial protection. The same empire that wrecked cities guarded the roads between them.

cards.headline: The Silk Road: understood
learned: A network of routes about 6,400 km long
Goods moved in stages through middlemen
The Pax Mongolica made the routes safer

questions.prompt: How did most goods cross the length of the Silk Road?

options.label: One caravan made the whole trip
The caliph’s royal post carried them
Ships took them around Africa
options.rationale: This was a network of land routes.

questions.explanation: Few people travelled the entire route; goods were handled in stages by middlemen.

questions.prompt: During the Pax Mongolica, what made long journeys across Mongol lands safer?

options.label: Relay stations and passes backed by imperial protection
The Mongols closed the roads to traders
options.rationale: They made the roads safer for traders.

questions.explanation: The Mongols expanded the yam stations, and merchants with paiza passes had imperial protection.

questions.prompt: Level 13’s Vikings brought home silver coins from Muslim Central Asia. Along the Silk Road, which way did silver travel?

options.label: West, with the silk
options.rationale: Silk went west; silver went the other way.

options.label: Nowhere: the road carried only silk
options.rationale: Wool, gold and silver moved too.

questions.explanation: On the Silk Road, silk went west while wool, gold and silver went east.
